why.why: The learner needs to run code in scripts and notebooks and use print() to see what the code is doing.
Formatted output with f-strings and converting text to numbers are everyday steps when working with data and model results.
Branching and loops, including enumerate and zip for pairing features with labels, are needed to read and write ML code.
Tuple unpacking (as in train_test_split), comprehensions and an understanding of aliasing and copying are needed to follow typical ML code.
Return values, keyword arguments, *args/**kwargs and docstrings are how scikit-learn functions are called and documented.
Reading tracebacks and common exceptions and debugging with print and assert are essential for fixing code that fails on real data.
The learner must install pandas and scikit-learn with pip and keep project packages apart in virtual environments.
scikit-learn models are objects of classes with shared interfaces, so understanding objects, classes, inheritance and duck typing explains what the code does.
Feature matrices are NumPy arrays, so indexing, slicing and boolean masks are needed to work with them.
Aggregation, broadcasting, reshaping, matrix multiplication, NaN handling and seeds underlie scaling, linear models and reproducible experiments.
Loading, inspecting, selecting, filtering and transforming columns with pandas is the core of loading data, and chained assignment is a common cleaning pitfall.
Cleaning data is a named part of the goal: missing values, types, duplicates, text, dates, categories and outliers.
Grouping and aggregating gives summaries by category that help in understanding a dataset before modelling.
Distributions, quick pandas plots and correlation heatmaps are how data is explored before training models.
The learner needs the core ideas of features, targets, train and test sets, overfitting and leakage to train models sensibly.
The estimator and transformer API, X and y, splitting, hyperparameters and random_state are how every scikit-learn model is used.
Scaling, encoding, imputing, column transformers and pipelines prepare cleaned data for models without leakage.
Regression models, their coefficients, regularization and metrics are a main use of scikit-learn.
Logistic regression, nearest neighbors, trees and probabilities are the standard classification models to train.
Training a classifier is only useful if it can be evaluated honestly, with baselines, confusion matrices, precision and recall, and AUC.
Cross-validation, hyperparameter search, learning curves and a final test set are how models are tuned and scored reliably.
Random forests and gradient boosting are strong, widely used scikit-learn models, and importances help explain them.
An end-to-end project and reading the scikit-learn documentation tie everything together and let the learner continue on their own.

note: No current level was given, so I picked the points the goal itself uses (pandas loading and cleaning, the scikit-learn workflow, evaluation) plus the Python and NumPy ideas needed to read ML code, and left prerequisites to the page. I left out files with the standard library, generators, string-only details, PCA and clustering, and other topics the goal does not use.
